fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Hermetic Baptism and a Roundabout Road to Paganism", "body": "McIntosh opens with what he now calls his hermetic baptism. At two or three years old, in the main quadrangle of Christ Church, Oxford, where his father lectured, he leaned too far over the fountain pool to watch the goldfish and fell in beneath the statue of Mercury, or Hermes, and his father hauled him out. He was never baptized as an infant, since both parents came from a nonconformist background, and when the usual age arrived he declined. Paganism, he notes, carries no doctrine of original sin to wash off, though it keeps rites of passage he believes the modern world has lost."}, {"title": "A Man of the Circle, Not the Straight Line", "body": "A rabbi's lecture McIntosh attended while living in New York gave him his sharpest distinction: in monotheism history runs in a straight line toward the second coming or the last judgment, while in polytheism everything moves in a great circle. He argues that this linear habit has migrated from religion into secular life, telling architects and artists never to look back, privileging the present over the past and eroding local cultural memory until only a global monoculture is left. Garton links it to Rene Guenon's The Reign of Quantity and the Signs of the Times, adding that uniformity is not unity."}, {"title": "Initiation by Scholarship in the Age Before the Internet", "body": "Asked whether study itself can initiate, McIntosh says scholarship was his way in, and that he never saw a conflict between being a scholar and a participant. His first book, written in his early twenties, was a history of astrology. Research before the internet meant rare volumes hunted at the British Library, the Watkins bookshop and the Atlantis shop in London, and trips abroad for manuscripts. A professor in Innsbruck sent him to a Masonic library in The Hague, whose Kloss collection held correspondence crucial to the thesis published as The Rose Cross and the Age of Reason."}, {"title": "Many Gods, One Source, and the Polytheistic Mind", "body": "Garton cites Augustine's City of God, where Augustine grants that the pagan gods exist but argues they are all facets of Jove, and asks whether the one and the many are two ways of seeing the same thing. McIntosh offers the Indian parallel of one supreme god with many deities beneath him, yet resists the monotheistic road because it ends in a uniform liturgy imposed everywhere. He praises James Hillman's Re-Visioning Psychology for arguing that polytheism reads the psyche better, since human beings are many people under one roof, and says he regards the gods as egregores raised by generations of shared worship."}, {"title": "Rune Circles, the Norns, and Gardens as Sacred Ground", "body": "McIntosh's practice is rooted in place. He has laid a circle of flat rune stones in his garden dedicated to the Norns, where shifting sunlight, a fallen leaf or a passing insect turns the circle into an oracle, and he practices stav, a Norwegian system of runic postures, daily. Skuld, the future Norn, is shown half veiled, which he reads as wyrd, a pattern that influences a life without wholly determining it. He credits the Scottish poet Ian Hamilton Finlay, whose Pentland Hills garden held image poems and an Apollo temple, with teaching him that tradition is a set of lessons, not a chain."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: The brilliant Dr. Christopher McIntosh returns to InnerVerse. In this free extended episode, we discuss his new book The Call of the Old Gods, and explore his "hermetic baptism" and early mystical initiation, the return of Paganism as a living tradition, the meaning of runes as oracles, cyclical vs linear time, ritual practice and initiatory experience, and how modernity erodes cultural memory.
fields.Quotes JSON: [{"text": "There's a divine distinction between doing what's right because you've been told by an authority versus going towards goodness for its own sake.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "When I heard that, I thought, well, I'm a man of the circle, not the straight line.", "author": "Christopher McIntosh", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/e25f1c65-0065-4a75-bdbe-b21604efbf70/CHRISTOPHER-MCINTOSH.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The qualitative worldview, the essential worldview, is that these essential qualities exist like a Platonic realm of forms that are condensed into material. It's a mirror to your soul. And so don't read it from the perspective of a student at university trying to get the right answers on the test.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "You'd be going down some back street in London and you come across a dusty bookshop where you might find some treasure for next to nothing.", "author": "Christopher McIntosh", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/e25f1c65-0065-4a75-bdbe-b21604efbf70/CHRISTOPHER-MCINTOSH.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "I do see synchronicity as the grammar structure of divine communication.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The thing is to accept the things that you can't change, but in the other areas where you're free to make changes, there you have the opportunity to shape your life.", "author": "Christopher McIntosh", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/e25f1c65-0065-4a75-bdbe-b21604efbf70/CHRISTOPHER-MCINTOSH.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}]
